You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: the small gray rubber cylinder becomes brown
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Has the small gray rubber cylinder been changed to brown while remaining identifiable as the same rubber cylinder?
node.criteria: Pass if the small rubber cylinder is visibly brown and retains its identity; fail if it remains gray or is visibly changed to a different color; unknown if the image does not provide enough evidence to judge its color or identity.
node.binding: Compare the small gray rubber cylinder in the image with the requested change: it must become brown while remaining a rubber cylinder.

node_traces.evidence: The small cylinder near the brown sphere changes from gray to brown, but in the edited image it has a visible hollow opening at the top, unlike the solid gray cylinder in the source. It therefore does not clearly retain its identity as the same rubber cylinder.

The small cylinder near the brown sphere is gray in the source and visibly brown in the edited image. It remains a small upright cylindrical object, with a hollow-looking top visible after the edit, so its identity as the same cylinder is retained.

The small cylinder near the brown sphere is gray in the source and brown in the edited image. It retains its short cylindrical form, with a visible hollow top, so it remains identifiable as the same rubber cylinder.

The small cylinder near the brown sphere is gray in the source and visibly brown in the edited image. It remains a small upright cylindrical object, with a hollow-looking top in the edited image, consistent with retaining its identity as the rubber cylinder.

The small cylinder near the brown sphere changes from gray to brown, but in the edited image it has a visible hollow opening and appears as a different, hollow tube rather than retaining the identity of the original solid rubber cylinder. The condition requires both the brown color and retained identity.

response.content: {"text":"The binding identifies the target and requested color, but its identity criterion is underspecified and invites inconsistent judgments: traces agree it turns brown, yet split on whether the visible hollow top means it is no longer the same cylinder. Refine the decision logic to distinguish observable evidence of a different object from a changed appearance, and to assess identity using the source-to-edit correspondence and stable features (location among the objects, approximate size, upright cylindrical form), without treating the hollow-looking top alone as decisive or ignoring it. Keep brownness and identity as separate checks, then apply the rubric’s partial-progress rule: a completed color change with genuinely unresolved identity is not automatically “no”; reserve failure for clear evidence the target was replaced or no requested change occurred, and use unresolved when the images cannot establish identity. The traces are valid observed executions with no dependency or transport failures, so this is a semantic/criterion-calibration issue. Their high-confidence disagreement despite the same evidence signals that the criterion needs clearer evidence thresholds, not that confidence should be lowered or the identity requirement removed."}
